title: Dover Mound, Mason County
summary: In Mason County, the Dover Mound was an Adena burial mound whose 55 burials William S. Webb and Charles E. Snow reported in their 1959 study.
bodyMarkdown:
The Dover Mound is an Adena burial mound in Mason County whose excavation added key evidence about one of the earliest mound-building cultures. Most of what is known about it comes from a single detailed report.

## The excavation and report

The archaeologists William S. Webb and Charles E. Snow of the University of Kentucky published [*The Dover Mound*](https://uknowledge.uky.edu/upk_archaeological_anthropology/1/) in 1959. According to the [University Press of Kentucky](https://www.kentuckypress.com/9780813155630/the-dover-mound/), the excavation uncovered 55 burials with their accompanying artifacts. The book reports this new data on the Adena in detail. Snow was a professor of anthropology and anatomy at the university.

Webb and Snow were already leading figures in Adena research. Their [earlier book](https://grokipedia.com/page/Adena_culture), *The Adena People* (1945), drew together evidence from Kentucky mound excavations. It outlined shared traits such as conical burial mounds and effigy pipes, while stressing differences from region to region.

## Who the Adena were

The Adena were a Native American society of the central and upper Ohio Valley, in parts of present Ohio, Kentucky, Indiana, West Virginia and Pennsylvania. The culture is [usually dated from about 600 BCE to 100 CE](https://grokipedia.com/page/Adena_culture), but chronologies vary by source and some evidence points to beginnings near 1000 BCE. The Adena belong to the Early Woodland period, a time marked by pottery, early gardening and monumental earthworks.

The culture is best known for its burial customs. Its people built conical burial mounds and geometric earthen enclosures that served as ceremonial centers. In Kentucky, Adena sites are found in the Bluegrass and in other parts of the state.

## Dating Dover

Radiocarbon dates from the Dover Mound help anchor the early Adena period. Early Adena communities, roughly 1000 to 500 BCE, [built simple conical mounds](https://grokipedia.com/page/Adena_culture) with log-lined tombs and basic grave goods. Radiocarbon tests from the Hartman Mound and the Dover Mound gave calibrated ranges from about 833–113 BCE to 1258–393 BCE.

Later Adena mounds, from about 500 BCE to 100 CE, grew larger and more elaborate. They held more burials, cremations and exotic goods such as copper ornaments and mica.

## Kentucky today

Like other protected sites, the Dover Mound is described here only as lying in Mason County. Webb and Snow's report remains available from the University Press of Kentucky, which reissued it in paperback in 2014. Other Adena places in Kentucky include the [Ashland Adena mounds](/stories/ashlands-adena-mounds/), the [Mount Horeb earthworks](/stories/mount-horeb-earthworks/) and the [Wright Mounds](/stories/wright-mounds-montgomery-county/). These mounds hold the remains of Native people and deserve care and respect.
